title: Wine Wimsey Review · Sun Nov 1 (extra)
subtitle: 14 feed (13 images + 1 TOBI at #7) and 4 stories, EXTRA batch for Sunday Nov 1 (made outside the regular daily run, so tomorrow's regular Nov 1 batch is separate) · CHARACTER: The Hot Mess (single-character mode) · 13 of 13 image posts are Scott's inbox quotes, word for word (#4 uses only the first line, see flag) · Captions: 5 SHORT, 8 SEE MORE · EXPERIMENT posts: #3, #6, #12 (pets, roadside outing) · FLAGS: #4 inbox item had a stray second line, #11 quote is wine as the subject, #3 mentions drinks and a drive so its picture has no wine glass and no car

posts.quote: To everyone who signed my 8th grade yearbook: you’ll be thrilled to know I did, in fact, stay cool.
posts.caption: I found the yearbook in a box marked misc that I packed in 2004 and never opened again. Inside, a boy named Dale had written never change in green ink, underlined twice, next to a drawing of a sunglasses face. I sat on the attic floor for forty minutes reading what people thought of me at thirteen. Most of it was about my hair. Three people wished me a great summer, which I did not have. I carried the book down the stairs holding the rail, because my knee has opinions, and put it on the shelf where it can think about what it did.
posts.first: The box also had a retainer, a cassette labeled Songs I Like, and a dried corsage that has outlived two cars and a dishwasher. I kept the corsage. It seemed rude to throw out something that stubborn. The yearbook went back on the shelf, spine out, in case Dale ever stops by.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting cross-legged on an attic floor, holding an open yearbook with a smug half-smile, a wine glass on a box beside her. Text in the speech bubble reads: To everyone who signed my 8th grade yearbook: you’ll be thrilled to know I did, in fact, stay cool.

posts.quote: I was just minding my own business, and the next thing I knew I was the same age as old people.
posts.caption: I sat down in the waiting room at 9:40 and realized I was reading the same large-print pamphlet as everyone else. We nodded at each other like a club. I have apparently been a member longer than I knew.
posts.first: The receptionist asked if I needed a pen and I produced two from my purse and a pencil from my hair. She said I was the most prepared person she'd seen all week. I took it as the compliment it wasn't meant to be.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in a doctor's waiting room, holding a clipboard and number ticket with wide eyes, older patients reading pamphlets behind her. Text in the speech bubble reads: I was just minding my own business, and the next thing I knew I was the same age as old people.

posts.quote: Skip going out for drinks. Let’s take a scenic drive, stop at little farm stands, and find a coffee shop in the middle of nowhere.
posts.caption: We found a stand outside of town with a cash box and a hand-lettered sign for cider donuts. Eleven dollars, two bags, no receipt. I have not felt this successful since the nineties.
posts.first: The woman at the stand asked if I wanted a bag and I said no, because I had already started eating. She nodded like that was the right answer. We did not speak again, and it was one of the better conversations I had all week.
posts.alt: Painted cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at an autumn roadside farm stand with pumpkins, apples and cider jugs, holding a coffee cup and a basket of apples with her eyes closed in a smile. Text at the top reads: Skip going out for drinks. Let’s take a scenic drive, Text at the bottom reads: stop at little farm stands, and find a coffee shop in the middle of nowhere.

posts.quote: Whatever you want to do, do it now. There are only so many tomorrows.
posts.caption: There is a list on my fridge titled Someday that has been up since the summer of 2019. It includes learning to make pie crust from scratch, driving up the coast, and finally reading the book my sister mailed me. The paper has curled at the corners and the magnet has slid down it like a tired guest. Last Tuesday I stood in front of it for a full minute holding a banana. I did none of it. I did eat the banana, which felt like a start. The list stays up. It has become part of the kitchen.
posts.first: My sister asked about the book last month and I told her I've read the first chapter four times, which is technically a lot of reading. She said that counts and also doesn't. We left it there. The book is on the nightstand, and it is very patient.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun standing beside a crossed-off wall calendar in a bedroom with her arms folded and a flat unamused stare, a wine glass on the nightstand. Text in the speech bubble reads: Whatever you want to do, do it now. There are only so many tomorrows.

posts.quote: My gut is never wrong. It might stick out a little, but that girl knows things.
posts.caption: Called it at 11:50 this morning. I said something was off about the lunch order, and it was off. Wrong sandwich, no pickle, and a bag of chips I never asked for. The gut sees everything.
posts.first: I've started consulting it before big decisions. Last week it said no to a new couch and yes to a second helping, and both turned out to be correct. Nobody at the table argued with it. It spoke at a very reasonable volume.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on a porch swing with a hand on her belly and a knowing side-eye smirk, a wine glass on a side table. Text in the speech bubble reads: My gut is never wrong. It might stick out a little, but that girl knows things.

posts.quote: If barking at nothing were a professional sport, my dog would be a world champion.
posts.caption: Biscuit has been barking at the same spot on the fence since six this morning. There is nothing there. I have checked it twice with my reading glasses on and once with them off, in case the problem was me. She turns, looks directly at me, and goes right back to it with new energy. At 7:15 I brought her a treat as a peace offering and she took it without breaking eye contact with the fence. At no point has she been wrong about the nothing. I've stopped checking. It's her fence, and she has clearly decided what's in it.
posts.first: I took her to the vet on Friday and the doctor said she is in perfect health with excellent lung capacity. I said I could have told him that. He wrote it down anyway. I think the medals would mostly be for the lungs.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a bag of treats beside a scruffy cartoon dog covered in gold medals in a sunny backyard, a wine glass on the fence post. Text in the speech bubble reads: If barking at nothing were a professional sport, my dog would be a world champion.

posts.quote: Somebody on my street is making a pot roast and I'm taking it personally.
posts.first: It started around ten and has been getting stronger since. I opened the window at eleven for the full effect. At noon I took a frozen casserole out of the freezer and set it on the counter to give the kitchen something to think about.

posts.quote: When you’re young and drop something, you just pick it up. When you’re older, you stare at it for a while and decide whether you really need it anymore.
posts.caption: I dropped a fork at 6:20 last night and it stayed there until this morning. I want to be clear that I saw it fall. I looked at it, it looked at me, and we both understood the terms. By 8 p.m. I had stepped around it three times, the way you do with a coat on a chair that has quietly become furniture. The dog was no help. At 7 this morning I finally bent down in three separate installments and picked it up. It's in the dishwasher now. Nobody has asked what took so long.
posts.first: My mother used to say you never bend down for just one thing. Last night I tried to find other things on the floor so the trip would be worth it. There was nothing else. The fork stayed where it was, completely unmatched.
posts.alt: Painted cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun standing in a kitchen with her arms crossed and head tilted, squinting down at a single fork on the tile floor, a wine glass on the counter. Text at the top reads: When you’re young and drop something, you just pick it up. Text at the bottom reads: When you’re older, you stare at it for a while and decide whether you really need it anymore.

posts.quote: Your secrets are safe with me because I honestly won’t remember them. Same goes for your birthday. Your birthday is very safe with me.
posts.caption: My sister told me something in confidence on Sunday and I remember a lowered voice, a serious face, and nothing else. I'm told it was important. It's very safe. I couldn't find it with a flashlight.
posts.first: I wrote her birthday on three different sticky notes this week. Two are on the monitor and one is stuck to my sleeve. She'll get a card on the correct day. Probably. The notes aren't confident about it either.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a cluttered home office desk covered in sticky notes, shrugging with her palms up and a sheepish grin, a cat asleep in the background. Text in the speech bubble reads: Your secrets are safe with me because I honestly won’t remember them. Same goes for your birthday. Your birthday is very safe with me.

posts.quote: The older I get, the more I get why a quiet yard full of birds beats a loud room full of people.
posts.caption: At 7:05 this morning I sat on the garden bench with a blanket and counted six sparrows, two finches, and one very rude blue jay. Nobody asked me for anything. The only sound was a feeder swinging on its hook and the occasional opinion from the jay. I stayed for forty minutes, which is longer than I've stayed at any party since 2016. A finch landed three feet from my slipper and looked at me the way a person does when they've decided you're fine. I got up cold and happy and a little bit smug.
posts.first: The jay came back around noon and took a peanut off the rail like he'd paid for it. I said good morning to him anyway. I'm not sure when I started greeting birds. My neighbor waved from across the fence and I waved back with the blanket still on.
posts.alt: Painted cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun wrapped in a blanket on a garden bench, smiling serenely with binoculars in her lap, finches and a blue jay at a bird feeder nearby, a wine glass on the bench arm, a cat asleep on the blanket. Text at the top reads: The older I get, the more I get why a quiet yard full of birds Text at the bottom reads: beats a loud room full of people.

posts.caption: Dinner was at 6:30 and nobody has been this proud of a plate since the third grade. Pasta, a salad nobody touched, and bread I did not bake. Everyone sat down at once, which is rare enough to mention.
posts.first: We used the good napkins, the ones from the drawer that only opens on holidays and when somebody is looking for the scissors. Nobody said anything about the napkins. I counted that as a win. The pasta stayed warm the entire time, which is a first.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a dining table with pasta, bread and salad, raising a wine glass in a triumphant cheer. Text in the speech bubble reads: Wine plus dinner equals winner.

posts.quote: I thought I rescued one cat. Turns out the first one left my house a five-star review on the Cat Distribution System.
posts.caption: The cat arrived on a Tuesday in March, in a laundry basket, with no paperwork. I told everyone I was fostering her for a week. That was three years ago. She has since taken the good chair, the warm spot on the dryer, and my side of the bed, and now she supervises dinner from the counter. Last month the neighbor's cat started coming by, and I'd swear the two of them held a meeting under the porch. I did not take notes. I wasn't invited. She's on the arm of the couch right now, watching me type this like a hostile editor.
posts.first: She knocked a glass off the counter at 3 a.m. for reasons she's keeping private. I swept it up in the dark with one slipper on. She watched from the doorway and did not offer to help. I think of it as a performance review.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on a couch with a grey cat in her lap holding a tiny card with five gold stars, giving a suspicious sideways glance, a wine glass on the side table. Text in the speech bubble reads: I thought I rescued one cat. Turns out the first one left my house a five-star review on the Cat Distribution System.

posts.quote: Since menopause, my body can gain weight from just about anything. I read the dessert menu, and my backside said, “Close enough.”
posts.caption: The waiter described the chocolate torte for a full ninety seconds and I have never listened to anything so closely. He used the word molten twice and feather once, and by the end I would have signed a lease. The rest of the table had already ordered coffee, which I took as a lack of vision. I asked him to go back over the salted caramel, and he did, slowly, with his hands, like a man giving directions to a lost relative. At no point did I look at the menu. I'd decided somewhere around molten. The torte arrived at 8:40 and was exactly as advertised.
posts.first: We split one dessert three ways. I ate mine and half of the other two while the table talked about the economy. Nobody noticed because the torte was apparently very persuasive. The waiter brought extra napkins without being asked, which told me everything.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in a restaurant booth holding up a dessert menu with wide eyes and a sly grin, a wine glass and candle on the table. Text in the speech bubble reads: Since menopause, my body can gain weight from just about anything. I read the dessert menu, and my backside said, “Close enough.”

posts.quote: Never underestimate a Gen X woman. We grew up figuring things out, then spent decades handling everything. Now we’re in our 50s and 60s and getting really good at deciding what isn’t our problem.
posts.caption: At fourteen I was left alone with a house key on a shoelace and a phone that was attached to the wall. I learned to make macaroni, fix the VCR, and deal with a rude adult on the line, all before dinner. Nobody gave me a medal. Nobody checked in. I did what needed doing and went outside until somebody called me in. That is how I ended up able to handle most things with one eyebrow. These days I look at a problem, decide whether it belongs to me, and close the door gently if it doesn't.
posts.first: Last week a coworker asked me to take over a project that was on fire and wasn't mine. I said I'd think about it and then I thought about it for exactly four seconds. The answer was no. I said it kindly and went back to my sandwich.
posts.alt: Painted cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in a laundry room doorway with her arms crossed and an unbothered smirk, pulling the door nearly shut on a pile of laundry, a wine glass on a shelf. Text at the top reads: Never underestimate a Gen X woman. We grew up figuring things out, then spent decades handling everything. Text at the bottom reads: Now we’re in our 50s and 60s and getting really good at deciding what isn’t our problem.
